prediction:
THOUGHT: This 3-month-old boy presents with a chronic (several weeks), erythematous, greasy yellow, scaly rash localized to the scalp and forehead — classic distribution for seborrheic dermatitis (commonly called “cradle cap” when on the scalp). The presence of greasy scales (not dry/flaky like in psoriasis or atopic dermatitis), lack of significant inflammation or pruritus, and absence of systemic symptoms align with benign, self-limited seborrheic dermatitis of infancy. The worsening in cold weather is consistent, as low humidity can exacerbate scaling. Although the father has psoriasis (a potential red flag for early-onset psoriasis), infantile psoriasis is exceedingly rare, typically presents with well-demarcated, thick, silvery plaques (not greasy/yellow), and often involves extensor surfaces or diaper area — not just scalp/forehead. The negative skin scraping (no fungal hyphae) rules out tinea capitis (which is also vanishingly rare in infants <6 months due to immature sebaceous gland activity and lack of fungal receptor expression). Atopic dermatitis usually presents later (often after 3–6 months), is pruritic, and tends to involve cheeks (in infants), flexural areas, or more widespread involvement — not isolated to sebum-rich areas like scalp/hairline/forehead. The prematurity (36 weeks) is not a risk factor for seborrheic dermatitis; rather, it’s common in otherwise healthy infants, possibly related to maternal androgen-driven sebaceous gland hyperactivity and Malassezia colonization (though not infectious in this age group). Normal CBC further supports a non-inflammatory, non-infectious etiology.

DIAGNOSIS: Seborrheic dermatitis
